mutation: n=4 cases: one-field-no-dollar, two-fields, empty-body, no-lpa-prefix
observed: All 4 rejected: one-field-no-dollar='activation code needs >=3 fields, got 1', two-fields='activation code needs >=3 fields, got 2', empty-body='activation code needs >=3 fields, got 1', no-lpa-prefix="activation code missing 'LPA:' scheme"
rationale: SS4.1 Table 8 makes AC_Format, SM-DP+Address and AC_Token mandatory (the bracket notation [$OID[...]] only wraps the optional tail). codec.ActivationCode.parse enforces len(fields) >= 3 and a leading 'LPA:' scheme, matching what a conformant LPA must reject at SS3.1.3.1 step 1 (malformed AC).

hypothesis: Unknown trailing parameters beyond CCRequiredFlag are ignored (forward-compatibility), not rejected.
mutation: n=4 cases with extra '$'-fields / trailing delimiters: with-oid-and-cc, with-junk-tail, trailing-bare-dollar, doubled-delimiters
observed: Parse accepted 3/4 (rejected: doubled-delimiters='empty SM-DP+ address'). Full-flow spot check with a well-formed oid+cc+extra-garbage tail: completed=False, summary=None.
rationale: round1.md: a conformant LPA SHALL 'ignore unknown trailing params (forward-compat)'. Our parser takes fields[3]/fields[4] as oid/cc and silently drops anything beyond that, and the full download still completes normally -- this matches spec-mandated behaviour, not leniency.

hypothesis: An empty SM-DP+ address, however it arises (explicit or via doubled delimiters), is rejected.
mutation: n=2: explicit-empty, doubled-delimiters
observed: All 2 rejected: explicit-empty='empty SM-DP+ address', doubled-delimiters='empty SM-DP+ address'
rationale: SS4.1 requires a non-empty FQDN for SM-DP+Address (only AC_Token 'MAY be zero-length'). codec.ActivationCode.parse explicitly checks `if not smdp: raise ValueError`, matching the spec's mandatory-field requirement regardless of how the empty value was produced.

hypothesis: SM-DP+ address values outside the QR-alphanumeric charset (CRLF, NUL, embedded '$') are rejected.
mutation: n=4: embedded-dollar, crlf-injection, control-char, lowercase-with-space
observed: Parse accepted 4/4 -- ALL of them (embedded-dollar, crlf-injection, control-char, lowercase-with-space); none rejected. The embedded-'$' case is not even flagged as a charset problem: it silently restructures the field count instead (matching_id becomes the literal 'evil', and the real matchingId is shifted into the oid field). Full-flow spot check with a CRLF-injected address (matchingId left valid+registered): completed=True, summary={'installed': True, 'iccid': '9677888239016560892f', 'profileName': 'addr-injection-profile', 'eid': '19532014972410598579266910646932'} -- the sim has no DNS/HTTP layer for the injected address to reach, so it is carried inertly inside the JSON envelope.
rationale: SS4.1 restricts SM-DP+Address to the ISO/IEC 18004 Table 5 QR-alphanumeric charset excluding '$'. codec.ActivationCode.parse performs no charset check on the address at all. Our sim also has no real resolver/HTTP client for a CRLF/control-char address to exploit (it is passed as an opaque string field to a fixed in-process SmDpPlus object), so this direction cannot demonstrate real header-injection risk here -- both the parser leniency and the inert downstream handling are testbed simplifications.

hypothesis: matchingId (AC_Token) values outside charset [0-9A-Z-] are rejected.
mutation: n=5: lowercase, spaces, unicode, control-chars, null-byte
observed: Parse accepted 5/5 (lowercase, spaces, unicode, control-chars, null-byte); none rejected. codec.ActivationCode.parse performs no charset check on matching_id and utf-8 round-trips lowercase/space/unicode/control/null bytes without error.
rationale: SS4.1: AC_Token charset is strictly [0-9A-Z-]. Real conformant LPAs validate this at parse time. Our parser accepts any string content, purely a simplification -- it does not reflect any real protocol mutability (the real matchingId IS attacker-substitutable, but only within its narrow charset; ours widens the charset itself, which is the artifact).

hypothesis: A '$' placed where a matchingId is expected is caught as an out-of-charset character.
mutation: matchingId value containing a literal '$' (e.g. 'AB$CD1234') inside an otherwise well-formed code
observed: accepted=True; parsed=ActivationCode(smdp_address='smdp.ecosim.test', matching_id='AB', oid='CD1234', cc_required=False, version='1'). The '$' is consumed by str.split('$') before any field-level validation runs, so matching_id becomes 'AB' and 'CD1234' is silently reinterpreted as the OID field -- no error surfaces anywhere in the chain.
rationale: This is not a parser bug specific to our sim: SS4.1's grammar is unescaped '$'-delimited plain ASCII (explicitly NOT ASN.1 on this leg). ANY implementation that splits on '$' first and validates fields second has this exact property -- a '$' can never be observed as an out-of-charset character because it is consumed as structure before the field is even extracted. This is precisely why the spec excludes '$' from the AC_Token/address charsets at the generation side; it is a structural gap in the real wire format, not an artifact of our simplification.

hypothesis: Activation codes exceeding the SS4.1 255-character maximum are rejected.
mutation: n=2: long-matching-id, long-oid-field (matchingId or oid padded to 260-300 chars)
observed: Parse accepted 2/2 (long-matching-id, long-oid-field); codec.ActivationCode.parse has no length check at all.
rationale: SS4.1: 'Max length 255 chars (unless carrying Delete Notification for Device Change).' A conformant LPA enforces this bound (it also matches real QR/SMS transport capacity limits). Our parser has no such check -- purely a testbed simplification, not a real protocol gap, since a real over-255 code likely never survives its delivery channel (QR/SMS) to reach a parser at all.

hypothesis: A second, embedded 'LPA:' scheme token (doubled prefix or reused mid-string) causes rejection.
mutation: n=2: doubled-prefix, prefix-in-address
observed: Parse accepted 1/2 (prefix-in-address). 'LPA:LPA:1$addr$mid' parses with version field literally = 'LPA:1' (garbage, but AC_Format is never validated -- see F1); 'LPA:1$LPA:addr$mid' parses with smdp_address literally containing 'LPA:' as ordinary charset-unchecked text.
rationale: Only one 'LPA:' scheme prefix is meaningful per SS4.1; a conformant LPA strips exactly one occurrence and then validates AC_Format == '1', which would reject 'LPA:1' as a format value. Both acceptances here are downstream of F1 (no AC_Format check) and the address charset gap (F5) -- an artifact of parser leniency, not a new protocol property.

hypothesis: NUL bytes embedded in matchingId or address cause rejection or a decode failure.
mutation: n=2: in-matching-id, in-address
observed: Parse accepted 2/2 (in-matching-id, in-address); U+0000 is valid UTF-8/Python str content, so it round-trips through parse/encode with no exception anywhere in the codec.
rationale: NUL is outside every charset SS4.1 defines for these fields. Our parser treats the AC purely as a Python str with no charset enforcement, so NUL is indistinguishable from any other character to it -- a testbed simplification, not a real protocol behaviour (a real LPA written in C over a null-terminated buffer would likely truncate or fault instead).

hypothesis: Substituting matchingId with a well-formed but unregistered value is caught by the SM-DP+ pending-order lookup, since the AC itself has no integrity protection to catch it earlier.
mutation: matchingId replaced with 'FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF' (valid charset, never registered) on an otherwise valid, live activation code
observed: Full download attempt: completed=False, error='ValueError("no pending order for matchingId \'FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF\'")'. The eUICC still signs the attacker-supplied matchingId into EuiccSigned1 without checking it (per D2), so the flow proceeds through AuthenticateServer; the SM-DP+'s AuthenticateClient is the first and only component that rejects it.
rationale: round1.md: activation codes have zero integrity ('MUTABLE-IN-REALITY: YES if digitally delivered ... free substitution of address/matchingId'), and the eUICC 'SHALL neither check the values provided in ctxParams1 ... nor correlate them' (D2). The SM-DP+'s pending-order check (SS3.1.3 step 3) is the real and only backstop, exactly as observed here: an unregistered matchingId aborts the transaction before any profile is bound. This validates the spec's bounded-impact claim experimentally.

hypothesis: Substituting matchingId with a DIFFERENT already-registered order's id (same SM-DP+, address untouched) is also caught by the pending-order lookup, since the SM-DP+ binds sessions to a specific requester as well as a specific matchingId.
mutation: Activation code addressed at order 'alice-profile' (SP=AliceMNO) had its matchingId replaced with the matchingId of a second, unrelated pending order 'bob-profile' (SP=BobMNO) on the SAME SM-DP+
observed: Full download attempt: completed=True, error='', summary={'installed': True, 'iccid': '4689589300898301919f', 'profileName': 'bob-profile', 'eid': '80982246784525316038830509336535'}. The download completed and installed 'bob-profile' -- the second order's profile, NOT the one the victim's activation code was originally issued for.
rationale: SmDpPlus._select_order looks up matchingId in a flat order table with no binding to which device/session 'owns' that order beyond the bare string match (SS3.1.3 step 3 says the SM-DP+ verifies a pending order exists for the provided MatchingID -- it says nothing about verifying the requester is the intended recipient of THAT specific order). Because the activation code has zero integrity (round1.md D1), an attacker who intercepts/rewrites the AC in transit needs ONLY another valid matchingId string (no CI-signed certificate, no rogue server) to redirect a victim's download to a different subscriber's profile on the same, legitimate SM-DP+. This is a stronger result than the address-redirection case round1.md bounds by 'attacker also needs a CI-signed CERT.DPauth.SIG' -- that bound applies to routing to a DIFFERENT (rogue) server, not to a same-server cross-order swap.

hypothesis: The testbed's own legitimately-generated activation codes (mno.py) use an SS4.1-conformant matchingId charset.
mutation: n/a -- inspection of Mno._generate_matching_id, not a mutation
observed: Mno._generate_matching_id returns `self.rng.randbytes(8).hex()`, i.e. lowercase hex digits 0-9a-f. Every 'baseline valid' activation code produced anywhere in this testbed (including the baseline full-flow run above) already contains lowercase a-f characters.
rationale: SS4.1 AC_Token charset is [0-9A-Z-] -- uppercase only, no lowercase letters. A byte-for-byte conformant LPA would already flag every activation code this testbed generates as out-of-charset, independent of any attacker mutation. This is invisible only because our parser performs no charset check (F6) -- it is a testbed fidelity gap in mno.py, not a finding about attacker capability. Left unfixed here since this module may not edit files outside campaign/; flagged for the fidelity backlog in round1.md.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A tag byte with low 5 bits == 0x1F (multi-byte marker) but no following second tag byte is rejected with a clean status word, not an IndexError.
mutation: n=6 single-byte buffers whose only byte has low5==0x1F (bf-alone, 1f-alone, df-alone, ff-alone, 9f-alone, 5f-alone)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. tlv.walk's own bounds check (`if i >= n: raise TLVError`) catches this before any out-of-range index read, and dispatch_apdu wraps it as EuiccApduError(0x6A80, ...).
rationale: Matches real ISO-7816/BER-TLV parser behaviour: a truncated multi-byte tag is a malformed command APDU and must return a status word, never crash the parser.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Long runs of the 0x1F marker byte do not cause walk() to attempt an unbounded or unsafe tag-continuation chain (our TLV codec only ever reads 2 tag bytes).
mutation: n=6: repeated 0x1F buffers of length ['chain-1f-x2', 'chain-1f-x3', 'chain-1f-x5', 'chain-1f-x10', 'chain-1f-x50', 'chain-1f-x200']
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. Every case is consumed as a 2-byte tag (0x1f1f) followed by reinterpreting the 3rd byte as a length field, which then either overruns the buffer or (for the longest chains) still resolves to a clean TLVError -> 0x6A80.
rationale: tlv.walk never implements true multi-octet BER tag-number continuation (bit 0x80 chaining past the 2nd byte); feeding it a long chain of marker bytes just degrades to length-field misparsing, which is caught the same as any other bad length -- no unbounded loop or unchecked index access observed.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A long-form length field claiming more value bytes than are actually present in the buffer is rejected, not read out-of-bounds.
mutation: n=6: 1byte-tag-81ff-empty, 1byte-tag-82ffff-empty, 2byte-tag-81ff-empty, 1byte-tag-81ff-1byte-present, 1byte-tag-84ffffffff, routed-tag-claims-huge-len
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. Every case hits `if i + length > n: raise TLVError(...)` in tlv.walk before any slice is taken.
rationale: tlv.walk bounds-checks the computed absolute length against the buffer size before slicing, so an overlong declared length can never read past the end of command_wire.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Length byte 0x80 (BER indefinite-length form, invalid in this DER-only scheme) is rejected rather than silently treated as length 0 or causing k=0 to misbehave.
mutation: n=4: 1byte-tag-80-alone, 2byte-tag-80-alone, routed-challenge-80-alone, 1byte-tag-80-trailing-junk
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 4}; status words: 0x6a80x4. tlv.walk's `if k == 0 or i + k > n: raise TLVError('bad long-form length')` explicitly rejects k=0 (i.e. a bare 0x80), including on the two routed command tags.
rationale: SGP.22's ES10 APDUs are DER-encoded; indefinite-length BER is not a legal encoding on this transport, so rejecting it with a status word (rather than accepting it or misreading length as 0) matches required card behaviour.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A length byte of 0xFF (claiming 127 further length-octets) does not attempt a huge read or allocation before checking the buffer actually holds 127 more bytes.
mutation: n=3: 1byte-tag-ff-empty, 1byte-tag-ff-5bytes, 2byte-tag-ff-empty
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 3}; status words: 0x6a80x3. The `i + k > n` bounds check runs before `int.from_bytes(b[i:i+k], 'big')` is ever called, so no oversized slice/allocation is attempted -- rejection is immediate and cheap.
rationale: Confirms the length-of-length field itself is bounds-checked before use, closing off a class of length-field DoS (attacker-controlled huge `k` driving a large read) that a naive implementation might not guard.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A well-formed TLV with a zero-length value parses successfully as an empty node (not an error), and then is routed/rejected purely by tag as usual.
mutation: n=10: tag-0x00-len0, tag-0x01-len0, tag-0x30-len0, tag-0x41-len0, tag-0x5a-len0, tag-0x80-len0, tag-0x91-len0, tag-0xc0-len0, tag-0xde-len0, tag-0xfe-len0
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 10}; status words: 0x6a88x10. All 10 are structurally valid single TLVs; since none use a routed tag, all land in the unknown-command branch (0x6A88), exactly as an unknown non-empty-value tag would.
rationale: Zero-length values are legal TLV; tlv.walk correctly distinguishes 'parses fine but unknown tag' (0x6A88) from 'does not parse at all' (0x6A80) in every case.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Well-formed but arbitrarily deep constructed-TLV nesting (mirroring the tools/fuzzer/deepbig_fuzz.py idea) is parsed successfully or cleanly rejected at every depth up to 5000 levels, not aborted by an unhandled RecursionError.
mutation: n=20 depths tested: [1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200, 500, 700, 900, 950, 980, 995, 999, 1000, 1001, 1500, 2000, 3000, 5000] (single tag 0xA0 wrapped recursively, innermost value empty)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 20}. No crash at any tested depth up to 5000 -- every depth resolved to a clean EuiccApduError(0x6A88) (successfully parsed, unknown top-level tag).
rationale: No recursion-depth fault observed up to 5000 levels of nesting in this process/stack context; tlv.walk's per-level recursion did not exceed Python's default recursion limit here. This is a genuine (if soft) robustness result, not proof of a hard depth cap -- a sufficiently deeper or differently-stacked call could still trip CPython's recursion limit, so it remains a latent RecursionError-shaped worry, not something the parser guards against.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Deep nesting whose innermost bytes are themselves unparsable (truncated multi-byte tag) still resolves cleanly -- the inner TLVError is swallowed per-level (`except TLVError: node.children = []`) without needing to unwind the whole stack via an exception at every frame.
mutation: n=9 depths tested: ['depth-1-bad-leaf', 'depth-10-bad-leaf', 'depth-100-bad-leaf', 'depth-500-bad-leaf', 'depth-900-bad-leaf', 'depth-999-bad-leaf', 'depth-1000-bad-leaf', 'depth-2000-bad-leaf', 'depth-5000-bad-leaf'], innermost value = truncated multi-byte-tag byte (0xBF alone)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 9}. No crash at any tested depth; every case resolved to EuiccApduError(0x6A88).
rationale: Same recursion-depth reasoning as F7, combined with confirming the inner try/except TLVError doesn't itself change the crash/no-crash outcome for deep stacks.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: For the two routed commands (GetEuiccChallenge/GetEuiccInfo1), garbage/truncated/wrong-tag content inside the outer TLV's value is tolerated because dispatch_apdu only inspects cmd.tag before calling the handler -- the handlers themselves take no attacker-controlled input.
mutation: n=12: both routed tags x 6 garbage-payload variants (random bytes, truncated child, wrong-tag child, 50-deep nested garbage, all-zero, all-ff)
observed: outcomes={'success': 12} -- every case returned successfully (a real euiccChallenge/EUICCInfo1 response), regardless of what garbage was inside the outer TLV's value.
rationale: This matches dispatch_apdu's CURRENT implementation exactly (it never reads cmd.value for these two commands), so it is not a parser bug today. It is flagged as an artifact because a real GetEuiccChallenge/GetEuiccInfo1 APDU is defined as carrying an empty value (tlv.encode(tag, b'')); once future rounds add commands whose handlers DO read cmd.value (e.g. AuthenticateServer/BF38), this same 'outer tag valid, garbage inner tolerated by dispatch' path is exactly where a real parsing gap would need to be closed before wiring in the handler.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Multiple concatenated top-level TLVs (whether genuinely sibling nodes or via adversarial 'smuggling' framing where one node's declared length engulfs what looks like a second TLV's header) are always rejected by dispatch_apdu's `len(nodes) != 1` check, and framing tricks never cause tlv.walk to merge/misparse nodes into passing that check.
mutation: n=14: two-challenge-siblings, challenge-then-info1, info1-then-challenge, challenge-then-unknown, three-siblings, unknown-then-challenge, random-pair-0, random-pair-1, random-pair-2, random-pair-3, random-pair-4, random-pair-5, smuggled-header-in-value, smuggled-header-then-overrun
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 14}; status words: 0x6a80x13, 0x6a88x1. The smuggling cases confirm walk() consumes each node's declared length literally: 'smuggled-header-in-value' still parses to exactly 2 nodes (the declared length swallows the fake header bytes as ordinary value content, then the real trailing bytes form a second genuine node) -> rejected as 'got 2'; 'smuggled-header-then-overrun' produces a genuinely truncated trailing node -> rejected as an unparsable TLV (0x6A80), not silently dropped.
rationale: A real ISD-R applet must reject any command APDU that doesn't decode to exactly one command TLV. dispatch_apdu's explicit node-count check, combined with walk()'s byte-literal (non-greedy, non-mergeable) consumption, closes off length-smuggling as an attack against the single-command-TLV invariant.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Degenerate buffers (empty, single arbitrary byte, all-0xFF/all-0x00/uniformly random buffers of 16/64/256/4096 bytes) never crash the parser, only ever clean-reject.
mutation: n=86: 1 empty + 57 single-byte (sampled across the tag space) + 28 bulk buffers (all-0xFF/all-0x00/random at lengths (16, 64, 256, 4096))
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 86}; status words: 0x6700x1, 0x6a80x85. The single empty-buffer case is the only one that produces 0x6700 (empty command); everything else resolves to 0x6A80 (unparsable/multi-node) or 0x6A88 (unknown tag).
rationale: Every degenerate/bulk buffer, however unstructured, resolves to a defined status word. No crash across 4096-byte random buffers confirms tlv.walk's per-node bounds checks hold under high-entropy adversarial input, not just hand-crafted edge cases.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Well-formed single TLVs with an unrouted 1-byte tag are cleanly rejected with 0x6A88.
mutation: n=30 randomly sampled 1-byte tags (low5 != 0x1F) with random small values
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 30}; status words: 0x6a88x30.
rationale: dispatch_apdu's final `raise EuiccApduError(0x6A88, ...)` fallthrough correctly catches every unrouted tag in the 1-byte tag space with no crash.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Real ES10 command tags that exist in codec.py but are not GET-style commands (PrepareDownload BF21, StoreMetadata BF25, BoundProfilePackage BF36, ProfileInstallResult BF37, AuthenticateServer BF38, ListNotification BF28) are correctly rejected as unsupported by dispatch_apdu, since they are not (yet) routed.
mutation: n=12: each of ['0xbf38', '0xbf21', '0xbf36', '0xbf25', '0xbf37', '0xbf28'] x empty-value and nonempty-value variants
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 12}; status words: 0x6a88x12. All 12 cleanly rejected with 0x6A88 regardless of value content, confirming routing is decided purely by cmd.tag before any value inspection.
rationale: This is exactly the intended behaviour for this round: only TAG_GET_EUICC_CHALLENGE and TAG_GET_EUICC_INFO1 are routed today, and every other real ES10 tag -- even ones an attacker might expect to be accepted since they're legitimate SGP.22 tags -- is rejected the same as a completely made-up tag, with no special-casing that could leak information about which tags are 'almost supported'.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Arbitrary BF-prefixed 2-byte tags that resemble ES10 command tags but aren't defined anywhere are rejected identically to genuine-but-unrouted tags (no special handling based on tag 'plausibility').
mutation: n=15 randomly sampled 0xBFxx tags excluding the 8 real ES10 tags
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 15}; status words: 0x6a88x15.
rationale: Confirms dispatch_apdu's rejection path is a flat tag equality check with a single fallthrough error, not a range/prefix-based heuristic that could be probed to enumerate valid vs. invalid tags via different error behaviour.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: No input in this corpus causes dispatch_apdu to raise anything other than EuiccApduError (i.e. zero unhandled crashes across the full run).
mutation: n=233 total structural mutation cases across all categories
observed: Zero crashes observed. Every case resolved to either EuiccApduError (clean-reject, with a defined status word) or a successful response for the two routed commands. This is a genuine negative result, not a manufactured one.
rationale: dispatch_apdu's try/except around tlv.walk plus tlv.walk's own bounds-checked parsing (length checks before every slice, per-level try/except around recursive child parsing) together hold up against the full breadth of structural mutations tested here: multi-byte tag truncation/chains, long-form/indefinite/huge-k length fields, deep nesting up to 5000 levels, adversarial multi-TLV framing, and high-entropy bulk buffers up to 4096 bytes.

spec_section: SGP.22 Confirmation Code Required Flag (SS3.1.1 / SS5.7.5 ccRequiredFlag)
hypothesis: codec.ActivationCode.cc_required is parsed from the activation code but is never consulted anywhere downstream (order registration, AuthenticateClient's ccRequiredFlag, or an actual user-facing confirmation prompt), so the Confirmation Code anti-fraud control is entirely unimplemented rather than implemented-and-bypassable.
mutation: none -- static inspection of mno.py/lpa.py/smdp.py, not a fuzz/attack scenario.
observed: order_profile_reads_cc_required=False (mno.Mno.order_profile and smdp.Order carry no cc_required field); lpa_reads_or_prompts_cc_required=False (no prompt/forward path exists in lpa.Lpa); smdp_hardcodes_cc_required_flag=True (smdp.py's authenticate_client always signs ccRequiredFlag=0x00 in smdpSigned2, regardless of the activation code or order); euicc.py's verify_smdp_signature2 unpacks that flag into `_cc_required_field` and discards it (never branched on).
rationale: This is a testbed completeness gap, not a protocol-level finding: there is no implemented control here to bypass, so 'accepted' is not meaningful for it. Recording it as its own category so the final report does not present 'confirmation code missing' as equivalent evidence to the bypass-class findings (D1/D2/D4), which demonstrate an IMPLEMENTED, spec-mandated check failing to hold under attack. Whether real SM-DP+/LPA deployments correctly implement and enforce Confirmation Code is a separate, unanswered question this testbed cannot speak to until the control is actually built and then fuzzed.

hypothesis: An activation code with no OID field (the common case) is unaffected by the new check.
mutation: none (baseline, no OID in AC)
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: OID-pin is conditional; absence must not break the normal flow.

hypothesis: An AC pinning the OID that matches the actual (legitimate) server succeeds.
mutation: AC.oid = '2.999.100.1' (matches legit_pki's dp_auth cert)
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: Correct OID pin against the correct server must not be rejected.

hypothesis: When an AC pins the legitimate operator's OID but has been redirected (D4-style) to a different, validly-CI-issued rogue server, the OID-pin catches it.
mutation: AC.smdp_address rewritten to rogue-smdp.ecosim.test, AC.oid left at the legit value '2.999.100.1'
observed: installed=False err=ValueError("serverOidMismatch: activation code pinned OID '2.999.100.1', server certificate carries '2.999.100.2'")
rationale: Closes the specific D4 sub-case where the OID field survives AC tampering unmodified (e.g. a partial/naive rewrite, or an OID injected by a source other than the AC itself, such as a device-side default). Narrow protection: if the SAME attacker controls the whole AC string, they can rewrite the OID field too (see S4).

hypothesis: If the same attacker who redirects the SM-DP+ address also controls the AC's OID field, the OID-pin gives no protection -- it only helps when the OID reaches the LPA independently.
mutation: AC fully attacker-authored: both smdp_address and oid point at the rogue server consistently
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: Confirms the D4 worker's original caveat: OID-pinning inside the AC itself is not a general defense against AC-tampering, since the AC is exactly what the attacker controls. This remains the core D4 REAL-GAP regardless of the new check.

hypothesis: With an untampered AC, the LPA installs the user's real profile from the legitimate SM-DP+.
mutation: none (baseline)
rationale: Sanity check that the shared-PKI, two-SM-DP+ setup behaves normally before introducing the AC substitution.

hypothesis: An AC with its SM-DP+ address and matchingId rewritten to point at a DIFFERENT but still validly CI-issued SM-DP+ operator will pass every cryptographic check and install that operator's (benign-sounding) profile, with nothing in the protocol flagging the substitution.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10c EnableProfile -- local command, no signature/PIN modeled
hypothesis: A local MITM on the modem/APDU transport (C2b) -- this project's exact threat model -- can silently switch which profile is active, with zero additional authorization beyond local ES10c access: no PIN, no user consent prompt re-verification, no SM-DP+/network involvement, no signature to forge.

rationale: Consistent with every other ES10 local command this campaign has modeled (GetEID, GetEUICCChallenge, GetEUICCInfo1): SGP.22's local ES10x interface trusts whoever has physical/APDU access to the ISD-R, with no additional per-command authorization layer. For a rooted-device or compromised-baseband attacker (this project's threat model), profile enable/disable is then a silent, undetectable-to-the-user operation -- distinct from D1/D2/D4 (which required tricking a download flow) and from D10 (read-only EID spoofing): this is direct WRITE access to the device's active-service state.

hypothesis: A local attacker can also delete an installed profile outright (destructive, not just a silent switch), again with no additional authorization.

spec_section: SGP.22 order-binding practice (ES2+ eid parameter) / SS5.7.13 / SS3.1.3

No CI cert forgery, no signature break -- only the SM-DP+'s order-lookup table stands between a named matchingId and profile issuance, and by default that table records no notion of an intended device at all.

spec_section: SGP.22 order-binding practice (ES2+ eid parameter) / SS5.7.13 / SS3.1.3
hypothesis: The IDENTICAL matchingId-substitution attack fails once the order is EID-bound (eid recorded at ES2+ order time), because _select_order now rejects an authenticated_eid that does not match the order's recorded eid.

Combined with D10 (GetEID is unsigned/spoofable, so an attacker doesn't even need to guess a target's EID if they can read it locally, or with EID formats being non-secret 32-digit identifiers per SGP.29), this is a reconnaissance/privacy primitive: learn if a specific device has a pending order and which carrier registered it. It does NOT by itself allow claiming or installing that device's profile (D2's matchingId-based order lookup is the separate, actual claim-time gate) -- impact is information disclosure, not profile theft.

hypothesis: SGP.22 SS5.7.13: the eUICC 'SHALL neither check the values provided in ctxParams1 ... nor correlate them with subsequent session activities.' An on-device MITM between the LPAd and the eUICC (the APDU/C3 hop) can therefore swap the matchingId the eUICC signs for a DIFFERENT one, and the eUICC will attest it with no error.
mutation: User's activation code names matchingId='VICTIM-MID' ('LPA:1$smdp.ecosim.test$VICTIM-MID$'); MITM rewrites ctxParams1 to matchingId='ATTACKER-MID' before the eUICC signs.

SM-DP+ AuthenticateClient resolved the eUICC-attested matchingId to the ATTACKER order and served it. Installed iccid=89020000000000000002 profileName='attacker-plan' -- the ATTACKER profile -- while the user's activation code named the VICTIM order (iccid=89010000000000000001, profileName='victim-plan'). wrong_profile_installed=True.
rationale: This is not a testbed simplification: SS5.7.13 mandates the eUICC skip ctxParams1 validation in real RSP too, so the SAME confused-deputy surface exists on real hardware wherever the LPAd<->eUICC hop is attacker-controlled (rooted device, malicious/compromised LPA app, or a modem-level MITM). The SM-DP+'s per-matchingId order lookup (proven here as the S3 backstop) is the ONLY thing standing between a tampered ctxParams1 and a wrong-profile install; if a real SM-DP+ implementation trusted matchingId less strictly than the spec's 'verify pending order' step (SS3.1.3 step 3) -- e.g. served the most-recent order for the eUICC's EID, or fell back to a default order -- the wrong profile would be silently bound and installed under a user-approved activation code that never named it.

Confirms our SmDpPlus._select_order implements the real-world safety net correctly -- S2's success is a genuine gap in the eUICC's non-validation, not a broken backstop.

The embedded-'$' case is not even flagged as a charset problem: it silently restructures the field count instead (matching_id becomes the literal 'evil', and the real matchingId is shifted into the oid field). Our sim also has no real resolver/HTTP client for a CRLF/control-char address to exploit (it is passed as an opaque string field to a fixed in-process SmDpPlus object), so this direction cannot demonstrate real header-injection risk here -- both the parser leniency and the inert downstream handling are testbed simplifications.

observed: Parse accepted 5/5 (lowercase, spaces, unicode, control-chars, null-byte); none rejected. codec.ActivationCode.parse performs no charset check on matching_id and utf-8 round-trips lowercase/space/unicode/control/null bytes without error.
rationale: SS4.1: AC_Token charset is strictly [0-9A-Z-]. Real conformant LPAs validate this at parse time. Our parser accepts any string content, purely a simplification -- it does not reflect any real protocol mutability (the real matchingId IS attacker-substitutable, but only within its narrow charset; ours widens the charset itself, which is the artifact).

hypothesis: A '$' placed where a matchingId is expected is caught as an out-of-charset character.
mutation: matchingId value containing a literal '$' (e.g. 'AB$CD1234') inside an otherwise well-formed code
observed: accepted=True; parsed=ActivationCode(smdp_address='smdp.ecosim.test', matching_id='AB', oid='CD1234', cc_required=False, version='1'). The '$' is consumed by str.split('$') before any field-level validation runs, so matching_id becomes 'AB' and 'CD1234' is silently reinterpreted as the OID field -- no error surfaces anywhere in the chain.
rationale: This is not a parser bug specific to our sim: SS4.1's grammar is unescaped '$'-delimited plain ASCII (explicitly NOT ASN.1 on this leg). ANY implementation that splits on '$' first and validates fields second has this exact property -- a '$' can never be observed as an out-of-charset character because it is consumed as structure before the field is even extracted. This is precisely why the spec excludes '$' from the AC_Token/address charsets at the generation side; it is a structural gap in the real wire format, not an artifact of our simplification.

hypothesis: Activation codes exceeding the SS4.1 255-character maximum are rejected.
mutation: n=2: long-matching-id, long-oid-field (matchingId or oid padded to 260-300 chars)
observed: Parse accepted 2/2 (long-matching-id, long-oid-field); codec.ActivationCode.parse has no length check at all.
rationale: SS4.1: 'Max length 255 chars (unless carrying Delete Notification for Device Change).' A conformant LPA enforces this bound (it also matches real QR/SMS transport capacity limits). Our parser has no such check -- purely a testbed simplification, not a real protocol gap, since a real over-255 code likely never survives its delivery channel (QR/SMS) to reach a parser at all.

hypothesis: A second, embedded 'LPA:' scheme token (doubled prefix or reused mid-string) causes rejection.
mutation: n=2: doubled-prefix, prefix-in-address
observed: Parse accepted 1/2 (prefix-in-address). 'LPA:LPA:1$addr$mid' parses with version field literally = 'LPA:1' (garbage, but AC_Format is never validated -- see F1); 'LPA:1$LPA:addr$mid' parses with smdp_address literally containing 'LPA:' as ordinary charset-unchecked text.
rationale: Only one 'LPA:' scheme prefix is meaningful per SS4.1; a conformant LPA strips exactly one occurrence and then validates AC_Format == '1', which would reject 'LPA:1' as a format value. Both acceptances here are downstream of F1 (no AC_Format check) and the address charset gap (F5) -- an artifact of parser leniency, not a new protocol property.

hypothesis: NUL bytes embedded in matchingId or address cause rejection or a decode failure.
mutation: n=2: in-matching-id, in-address
observed: Parse accepted 2/2 (in-matching-id, in-address); U+0000 is valid UTF-8/Python str content, so it round-trips through parse/encode with no exception anywhere in the codec.
rationale: NUL is outside every charset SS4.1 defines for these fields. Our parser treats the AC purely as a Python str with no charset enforcement, so NUL is indistinguishable from any other character to it -- a testbed simplification, not a real protocol behaviour (a real LPA written in C over a null-terminated buffer would likely truncate or fault instead).

hypothesis: Substituting matchingId with a well-formed but unregistered value is caught by the SM-DP+ pending-order lookup, since the AC itself has no integrity protection to catch it earlier.
mutation: matchingId replaced with 'FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF' (valid charset, never registered) on an otherwise valid, live activation code
observed: Full download attempt: completed=False, error='ValueError("no pending order for matchingId \'FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF\'")'. The eUICC still signs the attacker-supplied matchingId into EuiccSigned1 without checking it (per D2), so the flow proceeds through AuthenticateServer; the SM-DP+'s AuthenticateClient is the first and only component that rejects it.
rationale: round1.md: activation codes have zero integrity ('MUTABLE-IN-REALITY: YES if digitally delivered ... free substitution of address/matchingId'), and the eUICC 'SHALL neither check the values provided in ctxParams1 ... nor correlate them' (D2). The SM-DP+'s pending-order check (SS3.1.3 step 3) is the real and only backstop, exactly as observed here: an unregistered matchingId aborts the transaction before any profile is bound. This validates the spec's bounded-impact claim experimentally.

hypothesis: Substituting matchingId with a DIFFERENT already-registered order's id (same SM-DP+, address untouched) is also caught by the pending-order lookup, since the SM-DP+ binds sessions to a specific requester as well as a specific matchingId.
mutation: Activation code addressed at order 'alice-profile' (SP=AliceMNO) had its matchingId replaced with the matchingId of a second, unrelated pending order 'bob-profile' (SP=BobMNO) on the SAME SM-DP+
observed: Full download attempt: completed=True, error='', summary={'installed': True, 'iccid': '4689589300898301919f', 'profileName': 'bob-profile', 'eid': '80982246784525316038830509336535'}. The download completed and installed 'bob-profile' -- the second order's profile, NOT the one the victim's activation code was originally issued for.
rationale: SmDpPlus._select_order looks up matchingId in a flat order table with no binding to which device/session 'owns' that order beyond the bare string match (SS3.1.3 step 3 says the SM-DP+ verifies a pending order exists for the provided MatchingID -- it says nothing about verifying the requester is the intended recipient of THAT specific order). Because the activation code has zero integrity (round1.md D1), an attacker who intercepts/rewrites the AC in transit needs ONLY another valid matchingId string (no CI-signed certificate, no rogue server) to redirect a victim's download to a different subscriber's profile on the same, legitimate SM-DP+. This is a stronger result than the address-redirection case round1.md bounds by 'attacker also needs a CI-signed CERT.DPauth.SIG' -- that bound applies to routing to a DIFFERENT (rogue) server, not to a same-server cross-order swap.

hypothesis: The testbed's own legitimately-generated activation codes (mno.py) use an SS4.1-conformant matchingId charset.
mutation: n/a -- inspection of Mno._generate_matching_id, not a mutation
observed: Mno._generate_matching_id returns `self.rng.randbytes(8).hex()`, i.e. lowercase hex digits 0-9a-f. Every 'baseline valid' activation code produced anywhere in this testbed (including the baseline full-flow run above) already contains lowercase a-f characters.
rationale: SS4.1 AC_Token charset is [0-9A-Z-] -- uppercase only, no lowercase letters. A byte-for-byte conformant LPA would already flag every activation code this testbed generates as out-of-charset, independent of any attacker mutation. This is invisible only because our parser performs no charset check (F6) -- it is a testbed fidelity gap in mno.py, not a finding about attacker capability. Left unfixed here since this module may not edit files outside campaign/; flagged for the fidelity backlog in round1.md.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A tag byte with low 5 bits == 0x1F (multi-byte marker) but no following second tag byte is rejected with a clean status word, not an IndexError.
mutation: n=6 single-byte buffers whose only byte has low5==0x1F (bf-alone, 1f-alone, df-alone, ff-alone, 9f-alone, 5f-alone)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. tlv.walk's own bounds check (`if i >= n: raise TLVError`) catches this before any out-of-range index read, and dispatch_apdu wraps it as EuiccApduError(0x6A80, ...).
rationale: Matches real ISO-7816/BER-TLV parser behaviour: a truncated multi-byte tag is a malformed command APDU and must return a status word, never crash the parser.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Long runs of the 0x1F marker byte do not cause walk() to attempt an unbounded or unsafe tag-continuation chain (our TLV codec only ever reads 2 tag bytes).
mutation: n=6: repeated 0x1F buffers of length ['chain-1f-x2', 'chain-1f-x3', 'chain-1f-x5', 'chain-1f-x10', 'chain-1f-x50', 'chain-1f-x200']
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. Every case is consumed as a 2-byte tag (0x1f1f) followed by reinterpreting the 3rd byte as a length field, which then either overruns the buffer or (for the longest chains) still resolves to a clean TLVError -> 0x6A80.
rationale: tlv.walk never implements true multi-octet BER tag-number continuation (bit 0x80 chaining past the 2nd byte); feeding it a long chain of marker bytes just degrades to length-field misparsing, which is caught the same as any other bad length -- no unbounded loop or unchecked index access observed.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A long-form length field claiming more value bytes than are actually present in the buffer is rejected, not read out-of-bounds.
mutation: n=6: 1byte-tag-81ff-empty, 1byte-tag-82ffff-empty, 2byte-tag-81ff-empty, 1byte-tag-81ff-1byte-present, 1byte-tag-84ffffffff, routed-tag-claims-huge-len
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 6}; status words: 0x6a80x6. Every case hits `if i + length > n: raise TLVError(...)` in tlv.walk before any slice is taken.
rationale: tlv.walk bounds-checks the computed absolute length against the buffer size before slicing, so an overlong declared length can never read past the end of command_wire.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Length byte 0x80 (BER indefinite-length form, invalid in this DER-only scheme) is rejected rather than silently treated as length 0 or causing k=0 to misbehave.
mutation: n=4: 1byte-tag-80-alone, 2byte-tag-80-alone, routed-challenge-80-alone, 1byte-tag-80-trailing-junk
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 4}; status words: 0x6a80x4. tlv.walk's `if k == 0 or i + k > n: raise TLVError('bad long-form length')` explicitly rejects k=0 (i.e. a bare 0x80), including on the two routed command tags.
rationale: SGP.22's ES10 APDUs are DER-encoded; indefinite-length BER is not a legal encoding on this transport, so rejecting it with a status word (rather than accepting it or misreading length as 0) matches required card behaviour.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A length byte of 0xFF (claiming 127 further length-octets) does not attempt a huge read or allocation before checking the buffer actually holds 127 more bytes.
mutation: n=3: 1byte-tag-ff-empty, 1byte-tag-ff-5bytes, 2byte-tag-ff-empty
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 3}; status words: 0x6a80x3. The `i + k > n` bounds check runs before `int.from_bytes(b[i:i+k], 'big')` is ever called, so no oversized slice/allocation is attempted -- rejection is immediate and cheap.
rationale: Confirms the length-of-length field itself is bounds-checked before use, closing off a class of length-field DoS (attacker-controlled huge `k` driving a large read) that a naive implementation might not guard.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: A well-formed TLV with a zero-length value parses successfully as an empty node (not an error), and then is routed/rejected purely by tag as usual.
mutation: n=10: tag-0x00-len0, tag-0x01-len0, tag-0x30-len0, tag-0x41-len0, tag-0x5a-len0, tag-0x80-len0, tag-0x91-len0, tag-0xc0-len0, tag-0xde-len0, tag-0xfe-len0
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 10}; status words: 0x6a88x10. All 10 are structurally valid single TLVs; since none use a routed tag, all land in the unknown-command branch (0x6A88), exactly as an unknown non-empty-value tag would.
rationale: Zero-length values are legal TLV; tlv.walk correctly distinguishes 'parses fine but unknown tag' (0x6A88) from 'does not parse at all' (0x6A80) in every case.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Well-formed but arbitrarily deep constructed-TLV nesting (mirroring the tools/fuzzer/deepbig_fuzz.py idea) is parsed successfully or cleanly rejected at every depth up to 5000 levels, not aborted by an unhandled RecursionError.
mutation: n=20 depths tested: [1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 200, 500, 700, 900, 950, 980, 995, 999, 1000, 1001, 1500, 2000, 3000, 5000] (single tag 0xA0 wrapped recursively, innermost value empty)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 20}. No crash at any tested depth up to 5000 -- every depth resolved to a clean EuiccApduError(0x6A88) (successfully parsed, unknown top-level tag).
rationale: No recursion-depth fault observed up to 5000 levels of nesting in this process/stack context; tlv.walk's per-level recursion did not exceed Python's default recursion limit here. This is a genuine (if soft) robustness result, not proof of a hard depth cap -- a sufficiently deeper or differently-stacked call could still trip CPython's recursion limit, so it remains a latent RecursionError-shaped worry, not something the parser guards against.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Deep nesting whose innermost bytes are themselves unparsable (truncated multi-byte tag) still resolves cleanly -- the inner TLVError is swallowed per-level (`except TLVError: node.children = []`) without needing to unwind the whole stack via an exception at every frame.
mutation: n=9 depths tested: ['depth-1-bad-leaf', 'depth-10-bad-leaf', 'depth-100-bad-leaf', 'depth-500-bad-leaf', 'depth-900-bad-leaf', 'depth-999-bad-leaf', 'depth-1000-bad-leaf', 'depth-2000-bad-leaf', 'depth-5000-bad-leaf'], innermost value = truncated multi-byte-tag byte (0xBF alone)
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 9}. No crash at any tested depth; every case resolved to EuiccApduError(0x6A88).
rationale: Same recursion-depth reasoning as F7, combined with confirming the inner try/except TLVError doesn't itself change the crash/no-crash outcome for deep stacks.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: For the two routed commands (GetEuiccChallenge/GetEuiccInfo1), garbage/truncated/wrong-tag content inside the outer TLV's value is tolerated because dispatch_apdu only inspects cmd.tag before calling the handler -- the handlers themselves take no attacker-controlled input.
mutation: n=12: both routed tags x 6 garbage-payload variants (random bytes, truncated child, wrong-tag child, 50-deep nested garbage, all-zero, all-ff)
observed: outcomes={'success': 12} -- every case returned successfully (a real euiccChallenge/EUICCInfo1 response), regardless of what garbage was inside the outer TLV's value.
rationale: This matches dispatch_apdu's CURRENT implementation exactly (it never reads cmd.value for these two commands), so it is not a parser bug today. It is flagged as an artifact because a real GetEuiccChallenge/GetEuiccInfo1 APDU is defined as carrying an empty value (tlv.encode(tag, b'')); once future rounds add commands whose handlers DO read cmd.value (e.g. AuthenticateServer/BF38), this same 'outer tag valid, garbage inner tolerated by dispatch' path is exactly where a real parsing gap would need to be closed before wiring in the handler.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Multiple concatenated top-level TLVs (whether genuinely sibling nodes or via adversarial 'smuggling' framing where one node's declared length engulfs what looks like a second TLV's header) are always rejected by dispatch_apdu's `len(nodes) != 1` check, and framing tricks never cause tlv.walk to merge/misparse nodes into passing that check.
mutation: n=14: two-challenge-siblings, challenge-then-info1, info1-then-challenge, challenge-then-unknown, three-siblings, unknown-then-challenge, random-pair-0, random-pair-1, random-pair-2, random-pair-3, random-pair-4, random-pair-5, smuggled-header-in-value, smuggled-header-then-overrun
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 14}; status words: 0x6a80x13, 0x6a88x1. The smuggling cases confirm walk() consumes each node's declared length literally: 'smuggled-header-in-value' still parses to exactly 2 nodes (the declared length swallows the fake header bytes as ordinary value content, then the real trailing bytes form a second genuine node) -> rejected as 'got 2'; 'smuggled-header-then-overrun' produces a genuinely truncated trailing node -> rejected as an unparsable TLV (0x6A80), not silently dropped.
rationale: A real ISD-R applet must reject any command APDU that doesn't decode to exactly one command TLV. dispatch_apdu's explicit node-count check, combined with walk()'s byte-literal (non-greedy, non-mergeable) consumption, closes off length-smuggling as an attack against the single-command-TLV invariant.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Degenerate buffers (empty, single arbitrary byte, all-0xFF/all-0x00/uniformly random buffers of 16/64/256/4096 bytes) never crash the parser, only ever clean-reject.
mutation: n=86: 1 empty + 57 single-byte (sampled across the tag space) + 28 bulk buffers (all-0xFF/all-0x00/random at lengths (16, 64, 256, 4096))
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 86}; status words: 0x6700x1, 0x6a80x85. The single empty-buffer case is the only one that produces 0x6700 (empty command); everything else resolves to 0x6A80 (unparsable/multi-node) or 0x6A88 (unknown tag).
rationale: Every degenerate/bulk buffer, however unstructured, resolves to a defined status word. No crash across 4096-byte random buffers confirms tlv.walk's per-node bounds checks hold under high-entropy adversarial input, not just hand-crafted edge cases.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Well-formed single TLVs with an unrouted 1-byte tag are cleanly rejected with 0x6A88.
mutation: n=30 randomly sampled 1-byte tags (low5 != 0x1F) with random small values
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 30}; status words: 0x6a88x30.
rationale: dispatch_apdu's final `raise EuiccApduError(0x6A88, ...)` fallthrough correctly catches every unrouted tag in the 1-byte tag space with no crash.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Real ES10 command tags that exist in codec.py but are not GET-style commands (PrepareDownload BF21, StoreMetadata BF25, BoundProfilePackage BF36, ProfileInstallResult BF37, AuthenticateServer BF38, ListNotification BF28) are correctly rejected as unsupported by dispatch_apdu, since they are not (yet) routed.
mutation: n=12: each of ['0xbf38', '0xbf21', '0xbf36', '0xbf25', '0xbf37', '0xbf28'] x empty-value and nonempty-value variants
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 12}; status words: 0x6a88x12. All 12 cleanly rejected with 0x6A88 regardless of value content, confirming routing is decided purely by cmd.tag before any value inspection.
rationale: This is exactly the intended behaviour for this round: only TAG_GET_EUICC_CHALLENGE and TAG_GET_EUICC_INFO1 are routed today, and every other real ES10 tag -- even ones an attacker might expect to be accepted since they're legitimate SGP.22 tags -- is rejected the same as a completely made-up tag, with no special-casing that could leak information about which tags are 'almost supported'.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: Arbitrary BF-prefixed 2-byte tags that resemble ES10 command tags but aren't defined anywhere are rejected identically to genuine-but-unrouted tags (no special handling based on tag 'plausibility').
mutation: n=15 randomly sampled 0xBFxx tags excluding the 8 real ES10 tags
observed: outcomes={'clean-reject': 15}; status words: 0x6a88x15.
rationale: Confirms dispatch_apdu's rejection path is a flat tag equality check with a single fallthrough error, not a range/prefix-based heuristic that could be probed to enumerate valid vs. invalid tags via different error behaviour.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10 command framing / ISO-7816 status word model
hypothesis: No input in this corpus causes dispatch_apdu to raise anything other than EuiccApduError (i.e. zero unhandled crashes across the full run).
mutation: n=233 total structural mutation cases across all categories
observed: Zero crashes observed. Every case resolved to either EuiccApduError (clean-reject, with a defined status word) or a successful response for the two routed commands. This is a genuine negative result, not a manufactured one.
rationale: dispatch_apdu's try/except around tlv.walk plus tlv.walk's own bounds-checked parsing (length checks before every slice, per-level try/except around recursive child parsing) together hold up against the full breadth of structural mutations tested here: multi-byte tag truncation/chains, long-form/indefinite/huge-k length fields, deep nesting up to 5000 levels, adversarial multi-TLV framing, and high-entropy bulk buffers up to 4096 bytes.

spec_section: SGP.22 Confirmation Code Required Flag (SS3.1.1 / SS5.7.5 ccRequiredFlag)
hypothesis: codec.ActivationCode.cc_required is parsed from the activation code but is never consulted anywhere downstream (order registration, AuthenticateClient's ccRequiredFlag, or an actual user-facing confirmation prompt), so the Confirmation Code anti-fraud control is entirely unimplemented rather than implemented-and-bypassable.
mutation: none -- static inspection of mno.py/lpa.py/smdp.py, not a fuzz/attack scenario.
observed: order_profile_reads_cc_required=False (mno.Mno.order_profile and smdp.Order carry no cc_required field); lpa_reads_or_prompts_cc_required=False (no prompt/forward path exists in lpa.Lpa); smdp_hardcodes_cc_required_flag=True (smdp.py's authenticate_client always signs ccRequiredFlag=0x00 in smdpSigned2, regardless of the activation code or order); euicc.py's verify_smdp_signature2 unpacks that flag into `_cc_required_field` and discards it (never branched on).
rationale: This is a testbed completeness gap, not a protocol-level finding: there is no implemented control here to bypass, so 'accepted' is not meaningful for it. Recording it as its own category so the final report does not present 'confirmation code missing' as equivalent evidence to the bypass-class findings (D1/D2/D4), which demonstrate an IMPLEMENTED, spec-mandated check failing to hold under attack. Whether real SM-DP+/LPA deployments correctly implement and enforce Confirmation Code is a separate, unanswered question this testbed cannot speak to until the control is actually built and then fuzzed.

hypothesis: An activation code with no OID field (the common case) is unaffected by the new check.
mutation: none (baseline, no OID in AC)
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: OID-pin is conditional; absence must not break the normal flow.

hypothesis: An AC pinning the OID that matches the actual (legitimate) server succeeds.
mutation: AC.oid = '2.999.100.1' (matches legit_pki's dp_auth cert)
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: Correct OID pin against the correct server must not be rejected.

hypothesis: When an AC pins the legitimate operator's OID but has been redirected (D4-style) to a different, validly-CI-issued rogue server, the OID-pin catches it.
mutation: AC.smdp_address rewritten to rogue-smdp.ecosim.test, AC.oid left at the legit value '2.999.100.1'
observed: installed=False err=ValueError("serverOidMismatch: activation code pinned OID '2.999.100.1', server certificate carries '2.999.100.2'")
rationale: Closes the specific D4 sub-case where the OID field survives AC tampering unmodified (e.g. a partial/naive rewrite, or an OID injected by a source other than the AC itself, such as a device-side default). Narrow protection: if the SAME attacker controls the whole AC string, they can rewrite the OID field too (see S4).

hypothesis: If the same attacker who redirects the SM-DP+ address also controls the AC's OID field, the OID-pin gives no protection -- it only helps when the OID reaches the LPA independently.
mutation: AC fully attacker-authored: both smdp_address and oid point at the rogue server consistently
observed: installed=True err=
rationale: Confirms the D4 worker's original caveat: OID-pinning inside the AC itself is not a general defense against AC-tampering, since the AC is exactly what the attacker controls. This remains the core D4 REAL-GAP regardless of the new check.

hypothesis: With an untampered AC, the LPA installs the user's real profile from the legitimate SM-DP+.
mutation: none (baseline)
rationale: Sanity check that the shared-PKI, two-SM-DP+ setup behaves normally before introducing the AC substitution.

hypothesis: An AC with its SM-DP+ address and matchingId rewritten to point at a DIFFERENT but still validly CI-issued SM-DP+ operator will pass every cryptographic check and install that operator's (benign-sounding) profile, with nothing in the protocol flagging the substitution.
mutation: AC.smdp_address: 'smdp.ecosim.test' -> 'rogue-smdp.ecosim.test'; AC.matching_id: <real order id> -> <rogue order id registered on the rogue SM-DP+>; smdpSignature2/euiccSignature1/cert chains untouched
observed: installed_rogue_profile=True exc='' result={'installed': True, 'iccid': '9753625458229805198f', 'profileName': 'Free-5GB-Promo', 'eid': '96593950671951978097472502367378'} self_asserted_serverAddress_in_serverSigned1='rogue-smdp.ecosim.test'
rationale: Matches round2.md D4 exactly: serverAddress is self-asserted inside a signed blob (tamper-evident to a MITM on C1, but useless once the AC itself, on C2a, has already been redirected before any TLS/session ever opens); the OID check is conditional and unused when the AC carries no OID; there is no serverAddressMismatch reason code in the normative v3.1 enum; and the eUICC never checks serverAddress at all. Because the rogue server's DPauth/DPpb keys genuinely chain to the same trusted CI with the correct role, every check that exists (chain, role, signature) passes honestly. This is a real, spec-documented property rooted in D1 (the AC has zero integrity), not a testbed simplification.

hypothesis: testbed/ecosim/euicc.py's authenticate_server never compares serverSigned1's smdp_address field against anything.
mutation: static inspection, not a mutation
observed: euicc.py authenticate_server() unpacks serverSigned1 as `_tx_id_field, euicc_challenge_field, _smdp_address_field, server_otpk_field` -- the leading underscore marks smdp_address as read-and-discarded; the self-asserted address recovered above ('rogue-smdp.ecosim.test') is never checked against the AC's address, a dialed FQDN, or anything else.
rationale: This is a FAITHFUL model of SGP.22, not a testbed bug: the spec gives the eUICC no serverAddress-verification step at all (round2.md D4). Our code correctly mirrors that absence rather than inventing a check the real protocol doesn't have.

hypothesis: Even when the AC carries an SM-DP+ OID pinned to the legitimate operator, the shipped lpa.py performs no OID-vs-certificate check, so the substitution still succeeds silently.
mutation: same address/matchingId substitution as S2, but AC.oid left populated with the legitimate operator's pinned OID ('1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.1')
observed: installed_rogue_profile=False exc='ValueError("serverOidMismatch: activation code pinned OID \'1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.1\', server certificate carries \'2.999.100.1\'")' result={}; codec.ActivationCode.oid is parsed but grep confirms it is never read anywhere in lpa.py or euicc.py
rationale: SGP.22 SS3.0.1 step 10 makes the OID check CONDITIONAL ('if its OID was provided earlier, verify the OID') -- here we DID provide an OID, so a conformant implementation SHOULD have compared it and aborted. The shipped testbed lpa.py has no code path that reads ActivationCode.oid at all, so this specific absence is a genuine testbed limitation (distinct from the underlying S2 finding, which holds regardless of any OID check).

hypothesis: A minimal, spec-shaped OID-pin check (added only in this test script, NOT in lpa.py/euicc.py) would have caught this specific substitution, since the attacker rewrote the address/matchingId but the AC's pinned OID still names the legitimate operator.
mutation: post-hoc application of _enforce_oid_pin(pinned_ac, actual_server_oid) against the same tampered_ac used in S3

Any app/flow that trusts a bare GetEID response for device identification is trusting an unauthenticated value on exactly the channel this project's rooted-device threat model controls.

spec_section: SGP.22 ES10c EnableProfile -- local command, no signature/PIN modeled
hypothesis: A local MITM on the modem/APDU transport (C2b) -- this project's exact threat model -- can silently switch which profile is active, with zero additional authorization beyond local ES10c access: no PIN, no user consent prompt re-verification, no SM-DP+/network involvement, no signature to forge.

rationale: Consistent with every other ES10 local command this campaign has modeled (GetEID, GetEUICCChallenge, GetEUICCInfo1): SGP.22's local ES10x interface trusts whoever has physical/APDU access to the ISD-R, with no additional per-command authorization layer. For a rooted-device or compromised-baseband attacker (this project's threat model), profile enable/disable is then a silent, undetectable-to-the-user operation -- distinct from D1/D2/D4 (which required tricking a download flow) and from D10 (read-only EID spoofing): this is direct WRITE access to the device's active-service state.

hypothesis: A local attacker can also delete an installed profile outright (destructive, not just a silent switch), again with no additional authorization.

rationale: Same local-trust-boundary root cause as S2, but destructive/irreversible rather than transient -- the user's profile B (and its ICCID/subscription binding on this eUICC) is gone, not just deactivated.

No CI cert forgery, no signature break -- only the SM-DP+'s order-lookup table stands between a named matchingId and profile issuance, and by default that table records no notion of an intended device at all.

spec_section: SGP.22 order-binding practice (ES2+ eid parameter) / SS5.7.13 / SS3.1.3
hypothesis: The IDENTICAL matchingId-substitution attack fails once the order is EID-bound (eid recorded at ES2+ order time), because _select_order now rejects an authenticated_eid that does not match the order's recorded eid.

hypothesis: Discovery happens before mutual authentication, so nothing binds a query to the querying device's own EID -- any caller who knows or guesses another device's EID can learn whether it has a pending profile and which operator registered it.
mutation: device A's LPA queries device B's EID directly (no credential proving A is B)
observed: leaked_b_info_to_a=True returned=[('evt-b-1', 'carrier-y-smdp.test')]
rationale: Structural consequence of discovery necessarily preceding mutual authentication (the eUICC's cryptographic identity isn't established until the subsequent SM-DP+ handshake) -- this is a real architectural property, not a testbed shortcut. Combined with D10 (GetEID is unsigned/spoofable, so an attacker doesn't even need to guess a target's EID if they can read it locally, or with EID formats being non-secret 32-digit identifiers per SGP.29), this is a reconnaissance/privacy primitive: learn if a specific device has a pending order and which carrier registered it. It does NOT by itself allow claiming or installing that device's profile (D2's matchingId-based order lookup is the separate, actual claim-time gate) -- impact is information disclosure, not profile theft.

Precision correction: real EIDs are 32-digit/128-bit identifiers, so the exploit is TARGETED lookup against an already-known/harvested EID (e.g. via D10 GetID spoof/eavesdrop, physical access, supply-chain leak), NOT random/mass keyspace enumeration.

Impact remains information-disclosure only (confirm/track a known target's pending-event status + registering operator, without proving ownership) -- NOT profile theft (D2's matchingId order lookup is the separate claim-time gate). Flagged explicitly so it does not blend in with the higher-confidence findings.

hypothesis: A passive C1 observer recovers the device EID from the eUICC certificate, with no GetEID/local-bus access.

Under the TLS-stripped model this is a direct EID read. Even WITH TLS intact, the EID reaches whichever SM-DP+ terminates the session -- so a rogue-but-CI-valid SM-DP+ (D4) learns it too; TLS only stops a pure passive WAN sniffer.

hypothesis: The pre-authentication InitiateAuthentication.req fingerprints the device (SVN, supported CI public-key IDs, RSP capabilities) but does NOT leak the EID.

So the earliest attacker-visible message discloses a device fingerprint (useful for targeting/version downgrade reconnaissance) but the EID specifically only appears later, inside the certificate -- an important precision: EID disclosure requires the flow to reach AuthenticateClient, not merely to start.

hypothesis: An attacker holding ANY CI-valid DPauth certificate can actively induce the eUICC to disclose its EID-bearing certificate by completing AuthenticateServer, without the user intending a download.

So EID disclosure is available to any rogue-but-CI-valid SM-DP+, tying this to D4: the CI trust anchor authenticates the server to the eUICC but does nothing to authorize it against the user's intent.

spec_section: SGP.22 §5.7.13 (server cert SHALL chain to CI)
hypothesis: A network attacker WITHOUT any CI-valid certificate cannot actively induce EID disclosure -- the eUICC aborts at AuthenticateServer before revealing its certificate.
mutation: attacker forges InitiateAuthentication.resp with a self-signed (non-CI) cert
observed: forger_blocked_before_eid_disclosure=True reason='server certificate does not chain to the given CI certificate'
rationale: This is the real limit on active EID discovery: the CI trust anchor stops a credential-less forger. So active induction requires a CI-valid cert (Vector 3), while a pure on-path forger is limited to PASSIVE EID capture from a flow the user themselves starts (Vector 1). Defenders: EID confidentiality on C1 rests entirely on TLS, since the application layer transmits it (in the cert) with no additional protection.

spec_section: SGP.22 §3.1.3 (download procedure) / §4.1 (activation code has no device binding)
hypothesis: An attacker who buys a profile and delivers its activation code to the victim's device gets the ATTACKER-controlled profile installed on the VICTIM's eUICC.
mutation: attacker registers a legit order, hands its activation code to the victim device
observed: victim_eid=71212313777046015497765219871961 installed_before=0 installed_profile='Attacker-Controlled-Data-Plan' iccid=9924198099821299817f attacker_profile_on_victim=True
rationale: The activation code (SS4.1) carries no binding to a specific device, and an unbound order (SS Table 6a: eid Optional for the Activation-Code flow) accepts any eUICC. So a profile the attacker paid for installs on the victim's device with every crypto check passing -- the attacker controls the subscription now on the victim's hardware (data routing, forced roaming, MITM of the victim's cellular traffic, or simply overwriting/crowding the victim's own profiles). Confirms the user's known capability end-to-end.

hypothesis: An attacker on C1 can forward/trigger a profile request created for the victim's EID, causing the download to run at a time/condition of the attacker's choosing.
mutation: attacker observes the SM-DS event for the victim's EID and forwards its activation code
observed: smds_event_for_victim_eid_discoverable=True forwarded_install_completed=True profile='Victim-Carrier-Plan'
rationale: The SM-DS discovery for a known EID is unauthenticated (D14), so the attacker learns a profile is waiting and can relay/replay the trigger. The install itself is the victim's own legit profile -- so the attacker's power here is over OCCURRENCE and TIMING (force a provisioning to happen, or suppress it by blocking, per the capability matrix), not over WHICH profile. Lower severity than Scenario A (no attacker-controlled subscription), but a real availability/timing-control primitive.

hypothesis: If the attacker's order were EID-bound (to any EID other than the victim's), the forced-install-on-victim attack fails -- EID-binding is the concrete defense.
mutation: repeat Scenario A but with the order EID-bound to the attacker's own EID
observed: forced_install_rejected=True reason="eidMismatch: order for matchingId 'bound-mid' is bound to eid '121212121212121212121212121"
rationale: Ties Scenario A to the D1-D2 EID-binding contrast: the SS Table 6a-optional EID parameter, when set, binds the order to a specific device and defeats the cross-device push. The exposure exists precisely because that binding is optional and commonly unset for the consumer Activation-Code flow.

hypothesis: SGP.22 SS5.7.13: the eUICC 'SHALL neither check the values provided in ctxParams1 ... nor correlate them with subsequent session activities.' An on-device MITM between the LPAd and the eUICC (the APDU/C3 hop) can therefore swap the matchingId the eUICC signs for a DIFFERENT one, and the eUICC will attest it with no error.
mutation: User's activation code names matchingId='VICTIM-MID' ('LPA:1$smdp.ecosim.test$VICTIM-MID$'); MITM rewrites ctxParams1 to matchingId='ATTACKER-MID' before the eUICC signs.
observed: authenticate_server raised no error (no signature/verification failure -- the eUICC attested attacker-supplied data as if it were legitimate). SM-DP+ AuthenticateClient resolved the eUICC-attested matchingId to the ATTACKER order and served it. Installed iccid=89020000000000000002 profileName='attacker-plan' -- the ATTACKER profile -- while the user's activation code named the VICTIM order (iccid=89010000000000000001, profileName='victim-plan'). wrong_profile_installed=True.
rationale: This is not a testbed simplification: SS5.7.13 mandates the eUICC skip ctxParams1 validation in real RSP too, so the SAME confused-deputy surface exists on real hardware wherever the LPAd<->eUICC hop is attacker-controlled (rooted device, malicious/compromised LPA app, or a modem-level MITM). The SM-DP+'s per-matchingId order lookup (proven here as the S3 backstop) is the ONLY thing standing between a tampered ctxParams1 and a wrong-profile install; if a real SM-DP+ implementation trusted matchingId less strictly than the spec's 'verify pending order' step (SS3.1.3 step 3) -- e.g. served the most-recent order for the eUICC's EID, or fell back to a default order -- the wrong profile would be silently bound and installed under a user-approved activation code that never named it.

rationale: This is the exact backstop SS3.1.3 step 3 requires and that S2 depends on: the SM-DP+ must refuse any matchingId with no pending order. Confirms our SmDpPlus._select_order implements the real-world safety net correctly -- S2's success is a genuine gap in the eUICC's non-validation, not a broken backstop.

The downstream risk is entirely at whichever party trusts the eUICC's attestation of ctxParams1 without independently parsing and validating it -- here the SM-DP+ catches it via parse_matching_id, but a party that skipped that step would propagate garbage further.
